title: Army Veteran Demands Netflix Pull Operation Safed Sagar Over Flag Code Breach in Coffin Scene
excerpt: A retired Indian Army officer has called for the suspension of the widely praised Kargil War series after spotting an incorrect draping of the Tricolour on a martyr's coffin.
body:
• An Indian Army veteran has flagged a Flag Code violation in Netflix's Operation Safed Sagar, noting the Tricolour was draped incorrectly on Squadron Leader Ajay Ahuja's coffin, with the green band visible instead of saffron towards the head.
  • The veteran has demanded that Netflix suspend the series until the scene is digitally corrected and a formal apology is issued to the armed forces and the martyr's family.
  • The controversy comes weeks after the series premiered to widespread praise for depicting the IAF's role in the 1999 Kargil War, with guidance from Air Chief Marshal (Retd.) B.S. Dhanoa himself.
  • The incident echoes a pattern of OTT controversies in India, including the removal of Zee5's Satluj series last month amid similar objections over military portrayals.

Netflix's Operation Safed Sagar, the military drama that brought the Indian Air Force's role in the 1999 Kargil War to screens worldwide on August 7, now faces calls for suspension after an Indian Army veteran flagged a breach of the Flag Code of India in a pivotal scene depicting a martyr's funeral.

The veteran identified the error in the series' portrayal of the coffin of Squadron Leader Ajay Ahuja, the Kargil War hero whose sacrifice anchors the drama. According to the complaint, the Indian Tricolour was draped with the green band visible towards the head of the coffin, reversing the correct protocol. Under India's Flag Code, the saffron band must face the head when draping a national flag over a coffin, a detail that holds deep significance in military funerals.

Demands for Digital Correction and Apology

The retired officer has gone beyond merely pointing out the error, demanding that Netflix suspend streaming of the series until the scene is digitally corrected. He has also called for a formal apology from the production team, arguing that the oversight, in a series that claims to honour the armed forces, amounts to disrespect.

"Flags, protocols and symbols matter. But demanding the entire show be yanked offline turns a correctable error into a national crisis."

— Short Post editorial analysis

The controversy has divided opinion. Supporters of the veteran's position argue that any depiction of military funerals, especially one involving a real martyr, must adhere strictly to protocol. Others contend that while the error should be acknowledged and fixed, demanding a complete suspension of a series that otherwise serves as a respectful tribute is an overreaction.

A Series Built on Authenticity

The timing of the controversy adds to its sting. Operation Safed Sagar was developed with extensive military cooperation, including guidance from Air Chief Marshal (Retd.) B.S. Dhanoa, who led the Golden Arrows squadron during the actual 1999 operation and later served as Chief of the Air Staff. The series was filmed across operational Indian Air Force bases with access to real aircraft and infrastructure.

At the trailer launch in Mumbai, Alka Ahuja, the wife of the late Squadron Leader Ajay Ahuja, was present and visibly emotional. Lead actor Siddharth, who portrays Ahuja, broke down during the event. "Thank you so much for the permission to do this. We would not have done that without you," Siddharth told Mrs. Ahuja.

The production team, which includes director Oni Sen and creators Abhijeet Singh Parmar and Kushal Srivastava, had positioned the series as a labour of love built on first-hand consultations with IAF veterans and the families connected to the operation.

A Familiar Pattern for Indian OTT

The flag code row is the latest in a growing pattern of controversies targeting Indian content on streaming platforms. Just last month, Zee5 pulled its series Satluj within 48 hours of release amid objections over security concerns and political pressure. Netflix itself faced scrutiny in 2024 when its Kandahar Hijack series triggered an uproar over the portrayal of hijackers' code names, leading the Information and Broadcasting Ministry to summon company executives.

The recurring cycle follows a familiar trajectory: a historical portrayal draws objections over specific details, social media mobilisation amplifies the criticism, and calls for bans or suspensions follow, often before the producers have an opportunity to respond.

Digital Fix or Cultural Emergency

Industry observers note that the flag draping error, while legitimate, is a technical oversight that can be corrected digitally without pulling the entire series. Netflix has previously made post-release edits to content in response to concerns raised by government bodies and veterans' groups.

The broader cast of the series, including Jimmy Shergill as Wing Commander B.S. Dhanoa, Abhay Verma, Dia Mirza, and Adil Hussain, has been praised by critics and audiences alike. Reviewers have noted the series' blend of large-scale action with personal stories of the pilots and their families.

For diaspora audiences who have followed the series with pride, the controversy raises uncomfortable questions about the line between demanding accountability for genuine errors and reflexively reaching for bans. As one editorial noted, thicker skins make stronger nations, and better cinema.

Netflix India has not yet issued a public response to the veteran's demands. The medical examiner's protocols for flag draping are laid out in Part III of the Flag Code of India, 2002, which specifies that the saffron band should be at the head end of a coffin.
nri_angle: The controversy over Netflix's globally available Kargil War series resonates with diaspora viewers who watched it with patriotic pride and now face the debate over balancing accountability for flag code errors with supporting military tributes.
author: Diaspora Desk
